back: Infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry and susceptible host. Breaking any one link stops transmission, so practice aims at several links at once. Exam questions ask which action interrupts which link.

front: Which link in the chain does hand hygiene interrupt?
back: The mode of transmission. Gloves also interrupt it. Sterile technique and skin care protect the portal of entry, vaccination and nutrition strengthen the host, and cleaning and disinfecting equipment removes the reservoir. Match the action to the link.

front: How do droplet and airborne particles differ in size and travel?
back: Droplets are larger, expelled by coughing or sneezing, travel roughly within two metres and fall quickly. Airborne particles are much smaller, stay suspended and can travel across a room or through ventilation. This difference decides mask versus N95 respirator and room type.

front: What are Routine Practices and when do they apply?
back: The baseline infection control measures used with all clients, in all settings, at all times, whether or not an infection is known. Any person's blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, non intact skin and mucous membranes may carry organisms, so everyone is treated the same.

front: What is a point of care risk assessment?
back: Before every client interaction the nurse asks what task is about to happen, what exposure is possible and what barriers are needed. It determines gloves, gown, mask and eye protection and is repeated whenever the task or the client's condition changes.

front: What does respiratory etiquette require of clients and visitors?
back: Cover the mouth and nose with a tissue or elbow, discard the tissue immediately, clean hands afterward, and offer a mask to a coughing client in a waiting area. It applies to everyone, supported by signs, hand rub and tissues at entrances.

front: A client with uncontrolled diarrhea is in a shared room. What placement is preferred?
back: A single room with a dedicated toilet or commode whenever possible. When single rooms are scarce, priority goes to the client who poses the greatest risk of spreading infection, decided with the charge nurse or infection control practitioner.

front: What are the Four Moments for hand hygiene?
back: Before initial contact with the client or the client's environment, before any aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, and after contact with the client or the client's environment. Hands are also cleaned before putting on and after removing gloves.

front: When is alcohol based hand rub preferred and what concentration is used?
back: When hands are not visibly soiled. A 70 to 90 percent alcohol rub is quick, kills more organisms, is gentler on skin and can be placed at the point of care. Cover all surfaces and rub until dry, about 15 to 20 seconds. Do not wipe or wave dry.

front: A nurse leaves the room of a client with C. difficile diarrhea. Which hand hygiene method is correct?
back: Soap and running water. Alcohol does not reliably destroy C. difficile spores. The same applies to norovirus and to hands visibly soiled. Lather for at least 15 seconds, rinse, dry with a paper towel and use the towel to turn off the tap.

front: Which hand and nail practices increase risk in clinical areas?
back: Artificial nails, chipped polish and rings with stones harbour organisms and make hand cleaning less effective. Nails should be short, natural and clean. Cracked skin is a portal for organisms, so use employer approved moisturizers.

front: Why are hands cleaned before putting on and after removing gloves?
back: Gloves can have tiny defects and hands become contaminated during glove removal. Gloves are an addition to hand hygiene, never a replacement. The exam trap is the answer that uses gloves instead of cleaning the hands.

front: When should gloves be changed during care of one client?
back: Between tasks when moving from a dirty site to a clean site, for example from perineal care to a face wash, as well as between clients. Put gloves on just before the task, remove them as soon as it ends, and never wash and reuse disposable gloves.

front: When is a fit tested N95 respirator required, and what must the nurse do each time it is put on?
back: For airborne precautions and certain aerosol generating procedures. The respirator must be fit tested, and the nurse performs a seal check every time it is donned. A surgical mask does not protect against airborne organisms.

front: What is a common order for putting on PPE?
back: Gown, then mask or respirator, then eye protection, then gloves pulled over the cuffs of the gown. Policies vary slightly, so the exam favours the principle of covering skin and clothing completely before entering the room.

front: What is a common order for removing PPE and the guiding principle?
back: Gloves, eye protection, gown, then mask or respirator, followed by hand hygiene. Remove the most contaminated items first, since gloves and the outside of the gown are most contaminated. Hand hygiene follows immediately.

front: Where is the PPE removed for contact and droplet precautions versus airborne precautions?
back: For contact and droplet precautions, gloves and gown are removed before leaving the room. For airborne precautions, the respirator is removed after leaving the room and closing the door, so airborne particles are not drawn out with the nurse.

front: Which organisms need Contact Precautions and what do they include?
back: MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, norovirus and scabies. Include a single room when possible, gloves and gown on entering, dedicated equipment such as a stethoscope and thermometer, careful cleaning and limited client movement. Use soap and water for C. difficile and norovirus.

front: What are the requirements for Droplet Precautions?
back: Used for influenza, pertussis and many respiratory viruses. A single room is preferred and a surgical mask with eye protection is worn within two metres of the client. If the client leaves the room, the client wears a mask.

front: What are the requirements for Airborne Precautions?
back: Used for tuberculosis, measles and varicella. Place the client in a negative pressure airborne infection isolation room with the door closed. Staff wear a fit tested N95 respirator, and non immune staff do not care for measles or varicella clients. The client wears a mask outside the room.

front: A feverish, unimmunized child with a rash who recently travelled arrives at a clinic. What does the nurse do first?
back: Mask the child, move the child and mother to a private room away from others, and notify the physician, nurse practitioner or infection control team at once. Measles spreads through the air, so use a fit tested N95 if entering. Do not return the child to the waiting room.

front: A client has had antibiotic associated watery diarrhea and a C. difficile test is pending in a shared room. What is done first?
back: Start Contact Precautions right away without waiting for the result, and ask for a single room with a dedicated toilet or commode. Wear gloves and gown, wash hands with soap and water, and use a sporicidal cleaner. Waiting lets spores reach the roommate.

front: How do the diagnosis and the isolation sign relate?
back: Signs on the door show the type of precautions so staff and visitors know what to wear, but the diagnosis is not written on the sign. This respects privacy. Leaving the sign off is the wrong answer.

front: Why are protective measures used for clients with severely low white blood cell counts?
back: These clients are highly susceptible, so they are placed in a clean room and staff and visitors with colds or infections are kept away. The aim is to protect the client, not others, which is the reverse of usual isolation.

front: What is the correct action after using a needle?
back: Activate the safety engineered device immediately and place the sharp in a puncture resistant container at the point of use. Never recap by hand and never carry a used needle to a distant container. Replace the container when about three quarters full.

front: A nurse suffers a needlestick. What are the steps?
back: Wash the site with soap and water, flush mucous membrane splashes with water or saline, report immediately to the supervisor and follow the post exposure protocol including prompt medical assessment. Treatment is time sensitive, so do not wait until the end of the shift.

front: How do medical asepsis and surgical asepsis differ?
back: Medical asepsis, or clean technique, reduces the number and spread of organisms in everyday care. Surgical asepsis, or sterile technique, aims to eliminate all organisms and is used for procedures that break the skin or enter sterile areas, such as catheter insertion or central line dressing changes.

front: During a sterile dressing change, a sterile glove touches the bedside table. What does the nurse do?
back: Stop, discard the contaminated glove, perform hand hygiene and put on a new sterile glove. A sterile item that touches a non sterile surface is contaminated even if it looks clean. If in doubt, treat the item as contaminated and replace it.

front: What are the rules for working with a sterile field?
back: Keep sterile items above waist level and within sight, treat the outer edge of about 2.5 centimetres as contaminated, never turn your back on the field and never reach across it. An unsterile item touching the field means the field must be replaced.

front: Classify equipment as critical, semicritical and noncritical, with the level of processing needed.
back: Critical items enter sterile tissue or the bloodstream and must be sterilized. Semicritical items touch mucous membranes or non intact skin and need at least high level disinfection. Noncritical items, such as stethoscopes and blood pressure cuffs, touch intact skin and need cleaning and low level disinfection.

front: Why must cleaning come before disinfection or sterilization?
back: Organic material such as blood or tissue blocks disinfectants and sterilants from reaching the surface. Always clean first. Keep clean and dirty items separate, and never reprocess single use devices unless the manufacturer and employer allow it.

front: Which measures reduce catheter associated urinary tract infection?
back: Insert a catheter only when truly needed, use sterile technique, keep the drainage system closed, keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer necessary. Review the need daily.

front: How is central line infection prevented?
back: Perform hand hygiene, use sterile technique for dressing changes, clean the hub with the agency's antiseptic before access, and question daily whether the line is still needed. The portal of entry is the line itself, so protect it.

front: What role does a practical nurse play in antimicrobial stewardship?
back: Give antibiotics on time, collect cultures before the first dose when ordered, and report adverse reactions and diarrhea, which may signal C. difficile. Antibiotics should be used only when needed, at the right dose and duration, since overuse promotes resistance.

front: When must the nurse notify the infection prevention and control team?
back: When a client has a suspected communicable disease, when two or more clients on a unit have similar symptoms, or when an unusual pattern appears. Some diseases are reportable to public health, and any nurse who suspects one should notify the team promptly.

front: How should the nurse care for and teach a client on isolation?
back: Provide the same assessment and timeliness as any client and do not avoid the room. Group care, gather supplies before entering, keep call bells in reach, and offer phone or video contact since isolation can cause loneliness. Teach hand hygiene and respiratory etiquette, then have the client demonstrate.

front: Which two items are acceptable client identifiers before giving a medication, and which are never acceptable?
back: Use two of full name, date of birth, or health card or agency number. Room and bed numbers are never identifiers because clients move. The trap is an option that checks the room number or only says the name aloud.

front: Why should you ask a client to state their name and date of birth rather than saying the name and waiting for a yes?
back: A confused or hard-of-hearing client may agree to any name, so a yes proves nothing. Have the client state both identifiers, then compare them with the wristband and the medication record. The exam trap is the leading question.

front: When are the three label checks done against the order, and what are look-alike drug names a hazard for?
back: Check when taking the container from storage, when preparing the dose, and before giving it or discarding the packaging. Read the whole name and the strength, not the first letters, because look-alike and sound-alike names cause wrong-drug errors.

front: A prescribed dose matches the written order but is far above the usual range for an older client with poor kidney function. What next?
back: Stop and verify with the prescriber before giving it. A dose outside the safe range for age, weight, or kidney function is questioned even when it matches the order. Matching the order alone does not make a dose safe.

front: A client has trouble swallowing a prescribed extended-release tablet. Why is crushing it wrong, and what is the right action?
back: Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated forms releases the whole dose at once and can cause toxicity. Ask the pharmacist about a liquid or other suitable form and tell the prescriber. Never crush unless product information says it is allowed.

front: Why must charting happen after a medication is given and not before?
back: The record must show what actually happened. If you chart first and the client vomits or refuses the dose, the record is false. Document drug, dose, route, time, site if injected, and response, and chart refused or held doses with the reason.

front: A time-critical dose, such as insulin with a meal or an antibiotic for severe infection, will be late. What do you do?
back: Tell the RN or prescriber. Time-critical drugs have a narrow window around the scheduled time, unlike routine drugs that follow the agency's accepted window. Delay without notifying anyone is the trap, since late insulin or antibiotics can harm the client.

front: What does the right reason mean, and what does the right response mean?
back: Right reason means you can link the drug to a diagnosis or symptom, and you ask if you cannot. Right response means assessing whether it worked or caused harm, such as pain score after an analgesic or glucose after insulin.

front: An order is illegible and uses the abbreviation U for units. What should the practical nurse do?
back: Clarify with the prescriber before giving anything. Do not guess at an unclear abbreviation. U can be mistaken for a zero, which could cause a tenfold overdose, so it is on do-not-use lists along with QD.

front: How do routine, PRN, stat, and one-time orders differ in how you act on them?
back: A routine order continues until stopped, a PRN is given as needed for the stated reason using your assessment, a stat is given immediately, and a one-time order is given once. The trap is giving a PRN on a schedule without assessing.

front: When may a verbal or telephone order be taken, and what steps follow?
back: Only in urgent situations and within agency policy and regulatory standards. Write it down, read it back to the prescriber, confirm it, and obtain co-signature afterward. Treating a verbal order as routine convenience is the exam trap.

front: A client says a past rash after penicillin was mild and long ago. How do you treat that for your allergy check?
back: As a documented allergy. Do not decide on your own that it is not real. Compare the drug and its class against it, hold the drug if there is a conflict, and report to the prescriber before giving it.

front: A client says they get a rash with a type of antibiotic, but the allergy list is blank. What is the first action?
back: Withhold the drug, ask about the reaction and the drug involved, check the drug class, and report to the prescriber before giving anything. Update the allergy list per policy. Trusting the blank record over the client is a safety failure.

front: The ordered digoxin is due and the apical pulse is 52 with a hold parameter below 60. What do you do first?
back: Hold the dose, recheck the pulse for a full minute, assess for dizziness, nausea, or visual changes, and report to the prescriber or RN. A slow pulse may signal toxicity. Giving first and reporting later, or just charting a hold, is wrong.

front: Name situations in which a practical nurse holds a dose and reports.
back: Pulse or blood pressure below ordered limits before digoxin or a beta blocker, low glucose or not eating before insulin, unsafe swallowing, new rash or wheeze after a new drug, a high INR on warfarin. Holding never ends your responsibility to tell and document.

front: Why is the ventrogluteal site often preferred for an adult intramuscular injection?
back: It lies away from major nerves and vessels. Also never inject into inflamed or bruised tissue, inject slowly, and aspirate only if current agency policy says so. The trap is choosing a site by convenience rather than safety.

front: How do you tell infiltration from phlebitis at an intravenous site, and what is done for both?
back: Infiltration is fluid leaking into tissue, with a cool, swollen site. Phlebitis is vein inflammation with warmth, redness, and a hard cord. For both, stop the infusion and report. Check the site before each use.

front: How should a client take a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet, and why no water?
back: Let it dissolve under the tongue without swallowing, with the client seated. Sublingual and buccal drugs are absorbed through the mucosa, so washing them down defeats the route and delays the effect.

front: Why teach a client to rinse the mouth after using an inhaled corticosteroid?
back: Rinsing and spitting removes drug left in the mouth and prevents oral thrush, a fungal infection. This is a controller drug taken daily, so the teaching applies every dose, not only when symptoms appear.

front: What is the basic formula for a dose calculation, and what is the answer for 750 mg ordered with 250 mg tablets?
back: Desired dose divided by dose on hand, times the quantity the dose on hand is in. 750 divided by 250, times 1 tablet, equals 3 tablets. Convert units first, then check that the answer is reasonable.

front: An order is 750 mg and the stock is 250 mg in 5 mL. Use ratio and proportion to find the volume.
back: Set 250 mg is to 5 mL as 750 mg is to X mL. Cross-multiply: 750 times 5 divided by 250 equals 15 mL. A volume this size is plausible for an oral liquid, so the reasonableness check passes.

front: When is dimensional analysis the most useful calculation method?
back: When a problem needs several conversions at once, such as micrograms per kilogram per minute to millilitres per hour. Start with the unit wanted in the answer and multiply by conversion fractions until only that unit remains.

front: List the metric conversions and the weight conversion needed for most dose calculations.
back: 1 g equals 1000 mg, 1 mg equals 1000 mcg, 1 kg equals 1000 g, and 1 L equals 1000 mL. Pounds divided by 2.2 gives kilograms. Convert units before calculating, because mixed units cause tenfold and thousandfold errors.

front: Why write 0.5 mg and 5 mg, never .5 mg or 5.0 mg, and why write mcg in full?
back: A missed decimal point causes a tenfold error. A leading zero keeps 0.5 visible, and no trailing zero stops 5.0 being read as 50. The Greek-letter abbreviation for micrograms is on many do-not-use lists, so write mcg.

front: A child weighs 14 kg and the order is 5 mg per kg per day in two divided doses. What is each dose?
back: The daily dose is 5 times 14, which is 70 mg, so each dose is 35 mg. Then compare the daily amount with the usual maximum for the child. Forgetting to divide by the number of doses is the common error.

front: What is the pump rate for 1000 mL ordered over 8 hours?
back: 125 mL per hour, found by total volume in mL divided by time in hours. Pumps are set in mL per hour, whereas gravity infusions are counted in drops per minute using the drop factor.

front: Calculate drops per minute for 500 mL over 4 hours with a 15 drops per mL set.
back: Time is 240 minutes. 500 times 15 divided by 240 equals 31.25, rounded to 31 drops per minute. The formula is volume times drop factor divided by time in minutes. Converting hours to minutes is the step often missed.

front: Why does a microdrip set make millilitres per hour equal drops per minute?
back: A microdrip set delivers 60 drops per mL, and 60 drops per mL cancels the 60 minutes in an hour. This gives a quick check on your calculation. Standard macrodrip sets differ and use the printed drop factor.

front: Heparin 25 000 units in 500 mL is ordered at 1000 units per hour. What is the pump rate?
back: Concentration is 50 units per mL, so 1000 divided by 50 is 20 mL per hour. Find the concentration first, then the rate. Heparin is high-alert, so get an independent double check per policy.

front: Name core high-alert medications and the extra safeguards they need.
back: Insulin, heparin and warfarin, opioids, concentrated potassium chloride, chemotherapy, and sedatives. Safeguards include independent double checks, standardized concentrations, and careful monitoring. A calculation or rate that looks extreme should be stopped and verified.

front: What must you check before drawing up insulin and what do you do after rapid-acting insulin?
back: Check the insulin type, since onset differs, and use an insulin syringe marked in units, never a standard syringe. After rapid-acting insulin the client must eat soon, and you watch for hypoglycemia such as sweating, shakiness, and confusion.

front: What happens with concentrated potassium chloride, and what if you find a vial in ward stock?
back: It is never given as a rapid undiluted push. It must be diluted and infused slowly, because a bolus can stop the heart. Report and remove a concentrate vial found in the wrong place according to policy.

front: What do you assess before and after an opioid, and what do you do for slow breathing or increasing drowsiness?
back: Assess pain, respiratory rate, and sedation before and after. Hold the next dose and report at once if breathing is slow or the client is hard to wake. Plan for expected constipation with a bowel regimen as ordered.

front: After a medication error reaches a client, what is the first priority and what follows?
back: Assess the client and notify the RN, charge nurse, or prescriber at once so treatment can begin. Then disclose per agency policy, document facts in the chart, and complete an incident report. Never hide the error or wait to see if the client seems fine.

front: Should the incident report be mentioned in the client's chart, and should near misses be reported?
back: No, the chart records factual care and the incident report is a separate quality document not referenced in the chart. Near misses are reported too, since they show system weaknesses. Honest reporting is individual accountability within a learning culture.

front: A client's blood pressure is falling after a new drug and the practical nurse is unsure what to do. What is the best step?
back: Consult the RN, NP, or physician early. For unstable or unpredictable clients the practical nurse does not manage alone. A practical nurse unsure of a task asks and does not perform it until competence is confirmed.

front: Why is nitroglycerin given under the tongue, and what is the first-pass effect?
back: Oral drugs pass through the liver first, where part is broken down before reaching the rest of the body. Sublingual nitroglycerin avoids the liver, so it works quickly. This is also why some drugs need a higher oral dose than injected dose.

front: Why might a malnourished client or one with liver disease show a stronger effect from a usual dose?
back: Low albumin leaves more free, unattached drug, and only the free portion is active. The same logic means reduced liver metabolism lets drugs build up. For such clients, expect to check or reduce the dose rather than give it by habit.

front: Which groups metabolize drugs more slowly, and what is the practical consequence?
back: Older adults, clients with liver disease, and newborns, so drugs may accumulate. Some drugs and grapefruit juice also change liver enzymes and alter levels of other drugs. Expect dose review and closer monitoring for adverse effects.

front: Which finding should be reported before giving a drug cleared by the kidneys?
back: A drop in urine output or a rise in creatinine. Reduced kidney function lets drugs accumulate, which is common in older adults. Giving the usual dose without reporting is the trap, because excretion, not absorption, is the problem.

front: What does half-life mean, and why do narrow therapeutic range drugs need blood tests?
back: Half-life is the time for the blood level to fall by half. Digoxin, lithium, and warfarin have narrow ranges, so small changes cause toxicity or treatment failure. Blood tests such as levels and the INR guide dosing.

front: What is the difference between an agonist and an antagonist, with a bedside example?
back: An agonist activates a receptor and an antagonist blocks it. A beta blocker blocks beta receptors in the heart, slowing the rate and lowering blood pressure. An opioid activates opioid receptors, easing pain but also slowing breathing.

front: How do a side effect, an adverse effect, and a toxic effect differ?
back: A side effect is expected and usually minor, an adverse effect is harmful and unintended, and a toxic effect is harm from too high a level. Nausea alone is usually a side effect, whereas rash or swelling suggests allergy.

front: A client develops facial swelling, wheezing, hives, and a weak fast pulse after a drug. What is the priority?
back: This is anaphylaxis. Call for help, give epinephrine according to policy, give oxygen, and keep the client lying down unless breathing is easier sitting. Do not wait for the rash to progress before acting.

front: An older client on several drugs has a new fall and confusion. What should the practical nurse consider first?
back: A possible drug effect, such as sedation or low blood pressure, before assuming aging. Report it. Older adults have slower clearance and more sensitive brain and blood pressure responses, so teach slow rising and review the drug list.

front: Why is a usual adult dose dangerous for a child, and what must you confirm?
back: Children are dosed by weight and surface area, so an adult dose can be toxic. Always confirm the dose against the child's weight. Newborns also have immature liver and kidneys, so they accumulate drugs easily.

front: How should a practical nurse respond when a client mentions traditional medicines or natural health products?
back: Ask respectfully about all products used, record what you learn, and share it with the prescriber, because some interact with prescribed drugs. Dismissing or ignoring them is the trap, as is telling the client to stop them without review.

front: What is the main risk of acetaminophen, and what should clients be taught?
back: Liver damage from too much. Teach clients to count all sources, since many cold and combination products contain it, and to stay within the daily maximum. Alcohol and liver disease raise the risk, and a suspected overdose needs urgent care.

front: Why are NSAIDs a concern for older adults, those with ulcers, or those taking anticoagulants?
back: They can irritate the stomach and cause bleeding, harm the kidneys, raise blood pressure, and worsen heart failure. Give with food and watch these clients closely. ASA also blocks platelets, so it prolongs bleeding.

front: A child with a viral illness has a fever. Why is ASA avoided and what is the usual choice?
back: ASA carries a risk of Reye syndrome in children and teens with viral illness. Acetaminophen is the usual choice, within weight-based limits. ASA is a tempting but wrong answer on the exam.

front: Which opioid effect does not fade with time, and what must be planned?
back: Constipation. Expect it along with nausea and drowsiness, and plan a bowel regimen as ordered. Also teach clients not to combine opioids with alcohol or sedatives, and hold and report if breathing is slow.

front: Why may naloxone need repeated doses after an opioid overdose?
back: Its effect can wear off before the opioid does, so breathing can fail again. Call for help, support breathing, give naloxone per policy, and keep monitoring. Giving one dose and leaving is the trap.

front: A client on an ACE inhibitor develops swelling of the lips and tongue. What does it mean and what is done?
back: This rare but serious effect can block the airway and needs urgent care. Call for help and report at once. ACE inhibitors (names ending in pril) more commonly cause a dry cough, and both they and sartans can raise potassium and harm a pregnancy.

front: What do you check before giving a beta blocker, and what must clients not do?
back: Check pulse and blood pressure and hold per the order. Beta blockers (names ending in olol) can worsen wheezing in asthma and hide the fast heart rate that warns of low glucose in diabetes. Never stop them suddenly.

front: A client on furosemide reports cramps and weakness, has an irregular pulse, and had a low potassium result. What first?
back: Assess further, including vital signs and a full-minute pulse, then report promptly to the prescriber or RN. Low potassium from a loop diuretic can cause dangerous rhythm changes. Suggesting a banana, or giving the next dose, is unsafe.

front: How do furosemide and spironolactone differ in what you monitor?
back: Furosemide removes potassium, so watch for low potassium with weakness, cramps, and irregular rhythm. Spironolactone holds potassium in, so the concern is high potassium. Pick monitoring and teaching that matches the class, and weigh daily.

front: How should nitroglycerin be used and stored for angina?
back: Give one dose under the tongue at the first sign of chest pain, with the client sitting. Teach calling emergency services if pain is not relieved within the time set by the provider. Expect headache and low pressure, and store in the original dark glass container.

front: What are early digoxin toxicity signs, and what raises the risk?
back: Nausea, loss of appetite, visual changes such as yellow-green halos, and a slow or irregular pulse. Low potassium raises the risk. Check the apical pulse for a full minute before each dose and hold and report per the order.

front: For a client on any anticoagulant or antiplatelet, what bleeding signs do you assess and teach?
back: Bruising, nosebleeds, blood in urine or stool, black stools, and headache or confusion that might mean brain bleeding. Use soft toothbrushes and electric razors, and hold pressure longer. Report unexplained bleeding right away.

front: A client on warfarin asks for an over-the-counter pain reliever for a headache. What do you advise?
back: Check with a pharmacist or prescriber before any new product, since NSAIDs and ASA raise bleeding risk and heavy acetaminophen can raise the INR. Also assess the headache, because a sudden severe one on an anticoagulant may mean brain bleeding.

front: Why is metformin held around some contrast imaging or in poor kidney function?
back: It can cause lactic acidosis when kidneys clear it poorly. Metformin alone does not usually cause low glucose. Report persistent vomiting, since the dose may need holding. Sulfonylureas such as gliclazide are the ones that can cause hypoglycemia.

front: What are diabetic ketoacidosis signs, and what does sick-day teaching include?
back: Nausea, abdominal pain, fruity breath, and deep rapid breathing, on top of thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue. It needs urgent care. Sick-day teaching: keep taking insulin, drink fluids, check glucose more often, and call the provider if vomiting persists.

front: A client with asthma has used the quick-relief inhaler every two hours since morning. What does it suggest?
back: Poor control or a worsening attack. Assess breathing, oxygen saturation, and ability to speak, and report promptly to the prescriber or RN. Reassuring the client or increasing use is wrong, since frequent rescue use needs treatment review.

front: How do a quick-relief inhaler such as salbutamol and a controller inhaler differ in use?
back: Salbutamol is for sudden wheeze or breathlessness and can cause shaking and a fast heart rate. Controllers are taken daily for prevention. Teach technique: shake, breathe out, press and inhale slowly, hold about ten seconds, and use a spacer if needed.

front: Why must a client finish a prescribed antibiotic course, and why must leftovers never be shared or saved?
back: Stopping early can let resistant bacteria survive, and misuse drives antibiotic resistance. Leftovers must not be shared or saved because the drug may be wrong for another person or illness, so return them to a pharmacy. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections only, not viruses. Stopping when the client feels better is the trap.

front: A client on an antibiotic develops severe, watery, persistent diarrhea. What should you suspect and do?
back: Clostridioides difficile infection is possible. Report it and use contact precautions as directed. Do not treat it as a trivial side effect. Check allergy lists too, since penicillins and cephalosporins can cross-react.

front: Which findings together suggest sepsis, and why is timing important?
back: Fever, fast heart rate, low blood pressure, and confusion. Report promptly, because early and correct antibiotic administration is time-critical in serious infection. Waiting to see whether the client improves is the trap.

front: What should you watch for early in antidepressant treatment, and what is serotonin syndrome?
back: Watch for new or worsening suicidal thoughts, especially in younger clients and when a dose changes, and report them at once. Antidepressants may take weeks to work and must not be stopped suddenly. Serotonin syndrome means agitation, sweating, fever, tremor, and fast heart rate.

front: Why do lithium clients need steady salt and fluid intake, and what are signs of early toxicity?
back: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range, and dehydration raises levels. Early toxicity shows as tremor, nausea, and diarrhea, later confusion and unsteadiness. Regular blood levels guide dosing, so report these signs and do not give the next dose blindly.

front: Which drug classes must never be stopped suddenly, and what can happen if they are?
back: Beta blockers, corticosteroids, benzodiazepines, and anticonvulsants. Stopping steroids after long use leaves the body without its own supply, and stopping benzodiazepines or anticonvulsants can cause seizures. The wrong answer tells the client to quit when side effects appear.

front: What do you do during a seizure, and what should you never do?
back: Protect the head, loosen tight clothing, turn the client to the side after the movements stop, note time and features, and call for help per policy. Never put anything in the mouth.

front: How should levothyroxine be taken, and what signs suggest too much?
back: On an empty stomach, usually in the morning, apart from calcium or iron, and for life. Too much causes a fast heartbeat, tremor, and weight loss. Corticosteroids, by contrast, are taken with food and raise glucose and infection risk.

front: Why do heart and lung problems often appear together on the CPNRE?
back: Both systems form one oxygen delivery chain. A failing pump sends fluid back into the lungs, and failing lungs strain the heart. The trap is treating a breathing stem as only a lung problem; ask where the chain is broken.

front: A client can only say two or three words at a time, but the oxygen saturation looks acceptable. How serious is this?
back: Quite serious. Speaking only a few words at a time shows more respiratory distress than full sentences, whatever the number says. Trust the observed work of breathing and report, rather than being reassured by a single saturation reading.

front: Why compare vital signs with the client's own baseline, not only the textbook range?
back: Many clients live safely outside typical ranges, such as long term lung disease with lower saturation. A change from their usual is the real warning. The trap is calling a reading normal because it fits a table while it is a drop for this person.

front: Before adjusting oxygen for a client with long term lung disease, what must the practical nurse check?
back: The prescriber's order and the client's target saturation range. Oxygen is a drug, and these clients are often managed to a lower range. Raising flow because a number looks low compared with a healthy adult is the typical wrong choice.

front: What does very quiet or absent breath sounds in a client working hard to breathe mean?
back: It is a warning sign, not reassurance, because very little air may be moving. Treat it as an emergency, stay with the client and get help. The trap is reading quiet lungs as improvement in someone who still looks exhausted.

front: What do crackles and wheezes each suggest when you listen to the lungs?
back: Crackles, fine popping sounds, suggest fluid or secretions in small airways, as in heart failure or pneumonia. Wheezes, high pitched whistling, suggest narrowed airways, as in asthma or COPD. Report new sounds, and listen only within policy and competence.

front: A client with heart failure gains weight quickly overnight. What does this usually mean?
back: Fluid is being retained. In heart failure, rapid weight gain often comes before visible swelling or breathlessness. Weigh as ordered, compare with yesterday on the same scale, and report the gain, rather than waiting for symptoms to worsen.

front: What are the signs of left sided versus right sided heart failure?
back: Left sided failure sends fluid into the lungs: breathlessness, cough, crackles and trouble lying flat. Right sided failure sends fluid into the body: swollen ankles, swollen abdomen, distended neck veins and weight gain. Match the signs to the side.

front: A client with heart failure is short of breath and uncomfortable. What position helps most?
back: Upright, with the head of the bed raised or sitting in a chair. This lets the diaphragm move freely and eases fluid load on the lungs. The trap is lying the client flat for a procedure or comfort while breathlessness is worsening.

front: Why does a client taking furosemide need extra nursing attention?
back: Furosemide removes fluid through the kidneys, so the client urinates often and may become dizzy. Offer a toileting schedule, watch for dizziness and falls, and track intake, output and weight. Teaching the client to call before rushing to the bathroom prevents injury.

front: When should the nurse hold a heart rate or blood pressure lowering drug and report?
back: When the pulse or blood pressure falls below the limits in the order or the client's usual range. Always check both before giving these drugs. The practical nurse does not change doses, but holds per the order and reports promptly.

front: How should a client with heart failure be taught to weigh daily?
back: Weigh every morning after urinating and before eating, on the same scale, and report the gain amount the care team specified. Consistent conditions make changes meaningful. The trap is weighing at random times, which hides fluid retention.

front: How does angina differ from a heart attack?
back: Angina is chest pressure or heaviness from too little blood to the heart muscle, usually triggered by exertion or stress and eased by rest or nitroglycerin. A heart attack lasts longer, may not ease with rest, and means muscle begins to die.

front: A diabetic older woman reports unusual fatigue, nausea and feeling unwell but no chest pain. What is the safest approach?
back: Treat it as possibly cardiac until a qualified provider decides otherwise. Women, older adults and people with diabetes often lack classic chest pain. Take vital signs, stay with her and report. Assuming no pain means no heart attack is a classic trap.

front: A client on your unit reports chest pressure, sweating and nausea. What does the practical nurse do first?
back: Stay with the client, have them rest, and activate the emergency response, then take vital signs and follow the protocol. Time is heart muscle. Writing a note, offering an antacid or phoning family first delays urgent care and is wrong.

front: What details should be noted for a client with chest pain?
back: The exact time the pain started, how it feels, where it spreads, what the client was doing, and vital signs. This information guides the team. Record it after help is activated, never instead of calling for help.

front: If a client with prescribed nitroglycerin has chest pain, what must be rechecked after it is taken?
back: Blood pressure, because nitroglycerin can lower it and cause dizziness. Assist only within scope and the order, and keep the client seated or resting. The trap is giving it and leaving, ignoring a possible drop in pressure.

front: When is acetylsalicylic acid given in suspected heart attack, and when is it avoided?
back: It is given according to protocol or order, usually chewed. It is avoided if the client is allergic or has a bleeding problem. The practical nurse does not decide alone; follow the order or protocol and report allergies and bleeding history.

front: Why should a client with possible heart attack not be given food or drink?
back: They may need urgent procedures, and eating raises risk. Keep the client resting and do not leave them alone. The trap is offering water or a snack for comfort while waiting for help.

front: Why is hypertension called a silent condition, and what does it damage?
back: It often has no symptoms, so people feel well while it damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes over years. This is why clients must keep taking medication when they feel fine and why accurate measurement matters.

front: How should blood pressure be measured to avoid error?
back: Seat the client with back supported and feet on the floor, arm at heart level, after a few minutes of rest, using a correctly sized cuff. A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high reading, a common reason for wrong management.

front: Why teach clients on blood pressure medication to rise slowly?
back: Some drugs cause a drop in pressure on standing, called orthostatic hypotension, leading to dizziness and falls. Teach slow position changes, and report fainting or dizziness. The trap is telling clients to stop the drug when they feel dizzy.

front: A hypertensive client reports severe headache, vision change and weakness on one side. What is the right response?
back: Treat it as a possible emergency and report immediately, staying with the client. These signs may signal stroke or dangerous pressure. The trap is rechecking the blood pressure later or waiting to see whether the symptoms pass.

front: What is the difference between a reliever and a controller asthma medication?
back: A reliever such as salbutamol opens airways within minutes during symptoms. A controller, often an inhaled corticosteroid, lowers inflammation and is taken regularly even when well. Teach the difference, and report needing the reliever more than usual.

front: Why can too much oxygen harm a client with severe COPD?
back: It can reduce the urge to breathe and let carbon dioxide build up, causing drowsiness and confusion. Give oxygen as ordered, watch the response and report increasing sleepiness at once. Giving more oxygen to every breathless client is the trap.

front: A client with COPD on oxygen mask becomes very sleepy and the saturation is above target. What first?
back: Check breathing and airway, then reduce oxygen to the ordered level per policy and report immediately. Sleepiness may mean rising carbon dioxide. Only waking the client, or removing oxygen entirely without an order or assessment, misses the cause or risks hypoxia.

front: An older adult with pneumonia has new confusion but little fever. What should the nurse conclude?
back: Older adults with pneumonia often show confusion and little fever, so confusion is a sign of illness and low oxygen, not just aging. Check vital signs and saturation, and report. The trap is waiting for a fever before acting.

front: What nursing measures help a client with pneumonia?
back: Upright positioning, deep breathing and coughing, fluids if not restricted, oxygen and antibiotics as ordered, and monitoring for worsening. Routine Practices and any additional precautions protect others. Medication alone, without positioning and breathing support, is incomplete.

front: A client recently on bed rest after surgery has sudden breathlessness, sharp chest pain and a fast heart rate. What does this suggest?
back: Possible pulmonary embolism, a clot travelling to the lungs, which can follow immobility or surgery. Treat it as an emergency, stay with the client and report immediately. Observing for improvement before calling is the wrong choice.

front: What safety points apply when oxygen is in use?
back: Keep open flames and smoking away, post warning signs, check that tubing is not kinked and the device fits, and watch skin over the ears and nose for breakdown. With a non rebreather mask, the reservoir bag must stay inflated.

front: How does an incentive spirometer help after surgery?
back: It gives visual feedback on slow deep breaths, which prevents lung collapse and pneumonia. Use it regularly while awake, often about hourly as ordered, with coughing supported by a pillow over the incision. Shallow rapid breaths do not meet the goal.

front: What are the rules for suctioning a client?
back: Suction only when needed, using sterile or clean technique per policy, with limited suction time so oxygen does not drop. Watch heart rate and saturation, and stop if the client is distressed. Routine suctioning without need is the trap.

front: What early signs show a client is deteriorating before collapse?
back: A rising respiratory rate and heart rate, falling saturation, new restlessness or confusion, cool clammy skin, falling blood pressure and less urine. Restlessness and confusion are early signs of poor oxygen delivery, not behaviour problems or normal aging.

front: How should a practical nurse report a worsening client?
back: Use a clear structure: who the client is, what you found, what you did and what you need, then record exact values, times and who was informed. Consult the registered nurse or prescriber promptly, and never leave an unstable client if someone else can be sent.

front: How should inhaler teaching be done to make it effective?
back: Have the client demonstrate the steps and correct them, since many use inhalers poorly. A spacer improves delivery. Telling the client the steps once without a return demonstration is the trap. Also teach when to seek urgent help.

front: A client becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally. What are the first actions?
back: Call for help, start compressions and use an automated external defibrillator as soon as it arrives, following current Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada guidance. Do not leave the client to look for a colleague if someone else can be sent.

front: A client seems confused. What should the nurse check before concluding a thinking problem exists?
back: Check that the client can see and hear. Sensory loss is often mistaken for confusion or dementia. Glasses, hearing aids and clear communication come first. The trap is labelling a client confused when they simply cannot see or hear you.

front: Which neurological sign usually changes first and is the most sensitive?
back: Level of consciousness. A client who was alert and is now sleepy, restless, irritable or confused has changed, even if every other number is normal. Compare each assessment with the last one, because the trend matters more than a single value.

front: What does the Glasgow Coma Scale measure, and what does a falling score mean?
back: It scores eye opening, verbal response and motor response. A falling score means the client is getting worse. Use your workplace's tool and compare each score with the one before it, since the trend is more useful than any single number.

front: How are pupils checked, and which findings are an emergency?
back: Use a penlight in a dim room. Normal pupils are round, equal and constrict briskly. A pupil that becomes larger, slower or fixed, or new unequal pupils in a client who had equal ones, is an emergency sign requiring immediate report.

front: How does the nurse test strength and face symmetry in a quick neurological check?
back: Ask the client to squeeze both of your hands and push and pull with both feet, comparing sides, then smile, show teeth and stick out the tongue, watching for one sided drooping. Unequal findings are new weakness and must be reported.

front: A head injured client has rising blood pressure, a slowing heart rate and irregular breathing. What does this suggest?
back: Rising pressure inside the skull, a late and dangerous pattern. Report immediately and stay with the client. The trap is seeing a higher blood pressure and slower pulse as improvement because the heart rate looks calmer.

front: Why check blood glucose in any client with a sudden change in consciousness?
back: Low blood sugar can mimic stroke and is quickly treatable. Checking it takes little time and may fix the problem, but it must not delay calling for help when stroke signs are present. Check it while help is on the way.

front: What is the difference between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke?
back: Ischemic stroke is a blocked blood flow from a clot, and hemorrhagic stroke is a burst vessel. In both, brain cells start dying within minutes. Treatments for ischemic stroke work only within a limited time window after symptoms begin.

front: What does FAST stand for in stroke recognition?
back: Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness or drifting down, Speech that is slurred, confused or lost, and Time to call 9-1-1 right away. Other warning signs include sudden vision loss, severe headache, dizziness, loss of balance and confusion.

front: Why record the time a client was last seen well when stroke is suspected?
back: Stroke treatments depend on the time since onset, so this is among the most important facts to document. Note it, call for emergency help at once and report it. Estimating it later, or only telling the next shift, wastes the window.

front: A resident's blood glucose is 2.8 mmol/L. They are sweaty and confused but can swallow. What does the practical nurse do first?
back: Give a fast-acting oral carbohydrate, such as juice or glucose tablets, following the facility protocol, then recheck glucose in about 15 minutes and report. Treat the low glucose first rather than waiting for a callback.

front: Why is nothing given by mouth to a client who may have had a stroke?
back: Swallowing may be impaired, so food, fluid or oral medication can enter the lungs and cause choking or aspiration pneumonia. Wait for a swallowing screen following facility policy. Offering a drink to ease a dry mouth is the trap.

front: A client's stroke symptoms clear within minutes and they feel fine. What should the nurse do?
back: Treat it as a transient ischemic attack, a warning that a full stroke may follow, and arrange urgent medical assessment. Feeling better does not make it safe to wait. Reporting only if symptoms return is the wrong choice.

front: How should the weak arm of a stroke client be positioned and handled?
back: Support it on a pillow and avoid pulling on it when moving the client. This prevents shoulder injury and contractures. Pulling on the weak arm to turn or lift the client is the trap.

front: How does the nurse communicate with a client who has aphasia after stroke?
back: Use short clear sentences, give time to respond, and add gestures and pictures. Do not assume a client who cannot speak cannot understand. Speaking loudly, finishing sentences for them or talking over them to a family member is wrong.

front: What are the nurse's priorities during a generalized tonic clonic seizure?
back: Stay, note the start time, protect the head, lower the client to the floor, loosen tight neck clothing and clear hard objects. Never put anything in the mouth and never restrain. Turn the client onto the side once the jerking stops.

front: When should emergency help be called for a seizure?
back: If it lasts longer than the protocol limit, commonly about five minutes, if a second seizure follows without recovery, or if the client is injured, pregnant, diabetic, has trouble breathing afterward, or it is a first seizure. Do not wait to see if it stops.

front: Why is giving anti seizure medication on time a safety issue?
back: Missed doses are a common trigger for seizures. Give on schedule even when the unit is busy, and report missed or late doses. Delaying a dose because of workload is a classic trap on the exam.

front: An older adult on blood thinners hit their head but seems fine. What should the nurse do?
back: Observe at the ordered intervals, because bleeding can develop slowly over hours. Check consciousness, pupils, strength, headache and vomiting, and report any change. Assuming the client is fine because they look well at first is the trap.

front: Which signs after a head injury must be reported immediately?
back: Increasing drowsiness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, unequal pupils, weakness on one side, seizures, and clear fluid draining from the nose or ears. Any one of these may mean rising pressure or bleeding inside the skull.

front: How should a client with raised pressure inside the skull be positioned?
back: Keep the head of the bed raised as ordered, with head and neck in a neutral midline position, and avoid straining. Keep the client calm. Flexing or turning the neck sharply, or lying the client flat, can raise pressure.

front: A client may have a spine injury. What does the nurse do?
back: Do not move the client unnecessarily, maintain spinal alignment, and wait for help. Moving the client to a more comfortable position or sitting them up can cause permanent damage. Treat the suspicion seriously until cleared.

front: How does delirium differ from dementia in onset and course?
back: Delirium is a sudden change in attention and thinking over hours or days, with a fluctuating course, and has a treatable cause. Dementia is a gradual, progressive loss of memory and thinking. Sudden change in an older client is delirium until shown otherwise.

front: An 82 year old is suddenly agitated and picking at sheets, with dark smelly urine. What first?
back: Treat it as delirium, check vital signs, oxygen saturation and blood glucose, assess pain, bladder and bowel, and report promptly so the cause, perhaps a urinary infection, can be found. Calling it worse dementia and giving a sedative first is wrong.

front: What person centred approaches help a client with dementia during agitation?
back: Keep routines predictable, speak calmly and simply, approach from the front, make sure glasses and hearing aids are in use, and look for unmet needs such as pain, hunger or a full bladder. Avoid arguing with or correcting the client.

front: When may restraints be used for an agitated client?
back: Only as a last resort after less restrictive options have been tried, and following the law, policy and consent requirements. The first response is looking for unmet needs and treatable causes. Choosing a restraint or sedative first is the exam trap.

front: Why are levodopa doses for Parkinson disease time critical?
back: Late doses can leave the client stiff and unable to move or swallow. Give them on the client's own schedule and report late or missed doses. Delaying them because the unit is busy is an unsafe choice.

front: Which eye symptoms are emergencies needing urgent assessment?
back: Sudden vision loss, a curtain or shadow across the vision, new flashing lights or many new floaters, and severe eye pain with nausea. Report at once. Waiting to see whether sight returns can cost permanent vision.

front: How should eye drops be given safely?
back: Use clean hands and do not touch the dropper tip to the eye. Press lightly on the inner corner afterward to limit drainage into the nose, and wait a few minutes between different drops. For a chemical splash, flush with large amounts of clean water immediately and report.

front: How should you guide and orient a client with poor vision?
back: Introduce yourself, tell them when you enter or leave, describe what you will do, keep furniture in place, and let them hold your elbow while you walk slightly ahead. Describe food on a plate using a clock face. Moving belongings without telling them is the trap.

front: How should the nurse communicate with a client who has hearing loss?
back: Face the client, reduce background noise, speak clearly at a normal pace and slightly lower pitch rather than shouting, and use written notes if needed. Check that hearing aids are clean, working and in the ears. Shouting is the wrong answer.

front: Who should interpret for a client who uses sign language during consent?
back: A qualified interpreter, not a family member, for consent and sensitive discussions. Family members may filter, change or misunderstand information. Using the nearest relative because it is faster is the trap.

front: How can pain be assessed in a client who cannot report it reliably?
back: Use observational tools to look for grimacing, moaning, restlessness or guarding, and treat suspected pain per orders. Aphasia, confusion or low consciousness do not mean no pain. Assuming a silent client is comfortable is the trap.

front: What signs suggest swallowing difficulty, and what should the nurse do?
back: Coughing or choking while eating, a wet or gurgling voice after swallowing, food pocketed in the cheek, and drooling. Sit the client upright, offer small amounts, and stop and report if choking or voice change occurs. Follow ordered diet textures and thickened fluids.

front: What measures prevent falls in clients with neurological conditions?
back: Keep the call bell within reach, use a bed or chair alarm if in the care plan, keep the floor clear, use non slip footwear and answer calls promptly. Weakness, poor balance, sensory loss and medications all raise risk.

front: Why must neurological checks be repeated at the ordered interval and compared with the last?
back: A single normal set does not rule out slow decline. The trend reveals change from baseline. Keep checking and recording, report a drop in consciousness or new weakness, and stay with an unstable client while getting help.

front: In what order do you perform an abdominal assessment, and why does the order matter?
back: Inspect, auscultate, percuss, then palpate. Touching or pressing the abdomen first can change bowel sounds and give a false picture. The exam trap is palpating before listening, which makes the findings unreliable and may hurt a client.

front: How long must you listen in each quadrant before calling bowel sounds absent?
back: At least five minutes in each quadrant. Normal sounds are irregular gurgles every 5 to 15 seconds, so a short listen proves nothing. Absent sounds after surgery or with distension are reported, not simply recorded.

front: A client lies very still with a rigid, board-like abdomen and pain on release. What does the practical nurse do?
back: Report at once and stop further palpation. These are signs of peritonitis, an emergency. The trap is pressing deeper to confirm the finding, which causes pain and gains nothing the provider needs.

front: What does black, tarry, foul-smelling stool suggest, and what is your action?
back: Melena points to bleeding high in the GI tract, such as the stomach. Check vital signs, describe the stool in plain words and report promptly. The trap is treating it as a diet or iron effect without reporting it.

front: Why is bright red blood on the stool treated differently from black tarry stool?
back: Bright red blood suggests bleeding low in the tract or from the rectum, while black tarry stool means blood digested higher up. Both are reported. Record the amount, colour and time rather than guessing the cause.

front: A client vomits material that looks like coffee grounds. What does this mean?
back: It is partly digested blood, so bleeding is likely in the upper GI tract. Check vital signs, keep the client from eating or drinking and report immediately. Calling it ordinary vomit delays care for a possible bleed.

front: Why can pale, clay-coloured stool matter in a client with yellow skin and dark urine?
back: Clay-coloured stool can point to a bile duct or liver problem because bile colours normal stool. Together with jaundice and dark urine it is reported. The practical nurse describes the finding and leaves the diagnosis to the provider.

front: Right lower quadrant pain began around the navel and then moved. What might this suggest, and what do you do?
back: This pattern may suggest appendicitis. Report the pattern, keep the client from eating or drinking until told otherwise, and do not give a laxative or apply heat unless ordered. The nurse reports the pattern and the provider interprets it.

front: How should you weigh a client so the weights can be compared?
back: Use the same scale, at the same time of day, in similar clothing. Then a change reflects the client and not the method. Report a worrying trend, such as about 5 percent of body weight in a month, or follow facility policy.

front: How should a client be positioned for a meal and afterwards, and why?
back: Sit the client upright, ideally at 90 degrees, and keep them upright for at least 30 minutes after eating. This reduces reflux and aspiration. The trap is leaving a client reclined in bed to eat because it is easier for staff.

front: Which signs suggest dysphagia during a meal?
back: Coughing or choking with meals, a wet or gurgly voice after swallowing, food pooling in the cheeks, drooling and repeated chest infections. These raise the risk of aspiration pneumonia. Stop feeding, keep the client upright and report.

front: Why must you not thicken fluids by guesswork for a client with swallowing problems?
back: Texture and fluid thickness are set by a swallowing assessment, usually by a speech-language pathologist, and you follow the order exactly. Guessing can allow aspiration. The trap is changing a texture just to make the meal easier to serve.

front: A client coughs after each sip of thin fluid. Is carefully giving smaller sips an acceptable answer?
back: No. Stop feeding, keep the client upright, check airway and breathing and report so a swallowing assessment can be arranged. Smaller sips or a straw do not make swallowing safe. Technique changes never replace the assessment.

front: What must be done before every tube feeding or medication through a nasogastric tube?
back: Confirm tube placement by the facility method before each use. If placement is new or doubtful, report and have it verified before anything goes in. The trap is feeding because the tube was checked at the last shift.

front: Why is the head of the bed kept raised 30 to 45 degrees during tube feeding?
back: A raised position lowers the chance that formula flows back up and enters the lungs. Keep it raised during and for a period after feeding, as ordered. Lying flat during a feeding raises the risk of aspiration.

front: How should medications be given through a feeding tube?
back: One at a time, with the ordered water flush before, between and after. Never crush extended-release or enteric-coated tablets, and never mix drugs into the formula. Crushing these tablets can cause a dangerous overdose or block the tube.

front: During a tube feeding the client coughs, becomes short of breath and turns blue. What do you do first?
back: Stop the feeding right away, keep the client upright, call for help and assess breathing. Suspected aspiration is an emergency. Do not continue the feeding at a slower rate or wait to see whether the coughing settles.

front: What are the main risks of parenteral nutrition, and what does the practical nurse watch for?
back: It goes into a central vein and carries a high risk of bloodstream infection, so strict aseptic technique is needed. Watch for fever, chills, redness at the site and blood glucose changes, and report them promptly.

front: What teaching helps a client with gastroesophageal reflux disease?
back: Smaller meals, no eating within two to three hours of bedtime, a raised head of bed, limiting trigger foods and alcohol, stopping smoking and a healthy weight. The reason is less acid flowing back into the esophagus at night.

front: A client with burning behind the breastbone also has sweating, nausea and shortness of breath. Is this reflux?
back: Do not assume so. New chest pain with these symptoms is treated as possible cardiac pain and reported at once. The trap is giving an antacid and waiting, which delays care for a possible heart attack.

front: A client with a peptic ulcer has coffee-ground vomit, a fast pulse, low blood pressure and dizziness. What do you do?
back: Place the client flat or in a safe position, check vital signs, keep the client from eating or drinking, call for help and report immediately. These signs suggest significant blood loss. Giving an antacid and watching is not enough.

front: Why are clients on long-term NSAIDs taught to take them with food and report black stool?
back: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen irritate the stomach lining and can cause ulcers and bleeding. Food lessens irritation, and black stool is a warning of bleeding. Helicobacter pylori infection is the other common cause of ulcers.

front: What is the first priority when caring for a drowsy client who is vomiting?
back: Protect the airway by turning the client to the side. Then give ordered antiemetics, mouth care and small sips of clear fluid when permitted. Aspiration of vomit is the greatest immediate danger, ahead of fluid replacement.

front: Which features of vomiting must be reported urgently?
back: Vomit that is bloody, green or bile-stained, or projectile, or vomiting with severe pain and a rigid abdomen. These can signal bleeding, obstruction or peritonitis. Ordinary nausea with mild vomiting is managed with ordered measures and monitored.

front: In what sensible order are constipation interventions used?
back: Increase fluids unless restricted, add fibre gradually, encourage activity, offer toileting after meals with privacy and a footstool, and only then give ordered laxatives or enemas. The trap is going straight to an enema without trying simple measures or having an order.

front: Why is a bowel plan usually started when a client begins an opioid?
back: Opioids almost always cause constipation by slowing the bowel. Starting a plan early prevents hard stool and impaction. Teach clients that this effect is expected and to report when stool has not passed.

front: A client has leaking liquid stool but no true bowel movement for days. Do you give an antidiarrheal?
back: No. Liquid stool leaking around a hard mass is likely a fecal impaction, not true diarrhea. An antidiarrheal would make it worse. Report and obtain an order for the next step.

front: After caring for a client with C. difficile, why is soap and water used instead of alcohol hand rub?
back: C. difficile forms spores, and alcohol-based hand rub does not kill spores. Washing with soap and water removes them. Also use contact precautions, dedicated equipment and the spore-killing cleaner your facility names.

front: What are the main risks of diarrhea, and how is perianal skin protected?
back: Risks are dehydration, electrolyte loss, skin breakdown and spread of infection. Replace fluids as ordered, clean gently, apply a barrier product and record frequency and amount. Use contact precautions if infection is suspected.

front: A client has cramping pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen and no stool or gas. What is the safe action?
back: Hold food and drink, check vital signs and report at once. These signs suggest bowel obstruction, which can lose blood supply and perforate. The tempting but wrong answer is a laxative or enema.

front: Why should fever be reported early in a client with Crohn's disease on immune-suppressing drugs?
back: Immune-suppressing drugs raise the risk of infection and may hide the usual signs, so early fever matters. Care also covers hydration, nutrition and skin protection. Report a fever promptly instead of waiting to see whether it settles.

front: A client with liver disease becomes newly confused. What might this mean, and what do you do?
back: Confusion can mean ammonia is building up in the blood. It is a change in mental status that is reported without delay. Give medications carefully, report unusual drowsiness and never add over-the-counter products.

front: How are Sims position and the left side used for an enema, and why?
back: Position the client on the left side with the right knee bent. The descending colon is on the left, so gravity helps the solution flow. Give only with an order, stop for pain, bleeding or resistance and never force the tip.

front: What does a pale, dusky, purple or black stoma mean, and what should you do?
back: It may have a poor blood supply and is reported right away, not watched overnight. A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red. Reassessing it later instead of reporting is a common exam trap.

front: When is an ostomy pouch emptied, and how is the barrier opening cut?
back: Empty it when it is one third to one half full so its weight does not pull the seal loose. Cut the barrier opening about 2 mm larger than the stoma. Check the skin for redness, weeping or breakdown at each change.

front: How is a meal tray checked for a client with a documented food allergy?
back: Check the tray against the allergy listed on the client record every time, and never give the food. An allergy is not a preference. Follow allergy alerts and facility policy, and report any exposure or reaction immediately.

front: What urine output is reported promptly in an adult, and what is it called?
back: Less than about 0.5 mL per kilogram per hour, roughly under 30 mL per hour over several hours, is oliguria. It can mean dehydration, shock or kidney injury, so report it promptly. Do not simply encourage more fluids.

front: Why is a sudden weight gain of 1 kg in a day significant?
back: A 1 kg gain is about 1 L of retained fluid, and sudden weight gain is one of the most useful signs of fluid overload. Weigh daily when ordered, using the same scale, and report the gain along with swelling or breathlessness.

front: What does dark amber urine suggest, and what does red or tea-coloured urine suggest?
back: Dark amber suggests concentrated urine from low fluid intake. Red or tea-coloured urine suggests blood or muscle breakdown and is reported. Cloudy, foul-smelling urine suggests infection. Describe colour, clarity and amount instead of naming a diagnosis.

front: How should intake and output be recorded accurately?
back: Record everything in (oral, IV and tube feeds) and everything out (urine, vomit, liquid stool, drainage), measured in millilitres with a standard container. Estimating or leaving out items makes the record misleading for fluid decisions.

front: An older adult with a urinary tract infection may show which first sign instead of burning?
back: New confusion, a fall or loss of appetite may be the only sign. Report the change in behaviour. The trap is assuming a UTI always causes burning and dismissing confusion as simply age or dementia.

front: Which signs suggest a urinary infection has reached the kidney?
back: Fever, chills, flank pain and vomiting suggest kidney involvement, which is more serious and is reported urgently. A simple bladder infection causes burning, urgency and frequency. Do not wait for the next routine report.

front: A client has a swollen lower abdomen, small frequent voids and leaking urine. Is this incontinence?
back: It may be urinary retention with overflow leaking from an overfull bladder. Report the finding, use a bladder scan only if trained and obtain an order, since a catheter may be needed. Do not just provide incontinence products.

front: Where should the drainage bag of an indwelling catheter be kept?
back: Below the level of the bladder but off the floor, with tubing free of kinks and loops and the system kept closed. This allows downhill drainage and limits infection. Never disconnect the system for routine reasons.

front: Why is the need for an indwelling urinary catheter reviewed every day?
back: Catheters are a major source of infection, so they are used only with an order and a clear reason. Early removal prevents infection. If the catheter is no longer needed, report so removal can be ordered.

front: A client's urine output is falling. Why is encouraging extra drinking the wrong answer?
back: In acute kidney injury or heart failure, the kidneys may be unable to remove extra fluid, which can cause overload. Report the falling output and wait for direction. Causes can include dehydration, bleeding, infection or a blockage.

front: Why are arm veins protected in a client with chronic kidney disease?
back: They may be needed later for dialysis access. Avoid unnecessary needle sticks in those veins. Care also includes ordered medications, fluid and diet limits and teaching the client to report weight gain and breathlessness.

front: What do you check on a hemodialysis fistula, and what if it is absent?
back: Feel for a vibration (thrill) and listen for a whooshing sound (bruit) at least once per shift as policy states. If either is absent, report at once because the access may be clotted. Do not massage or compress the arm.

front: Why must you never take blood pressure or draw blood in the arm with a fistula?
back: Pressure or punctures can damage or clot the access that the client depends on for dialysis. The arm is protected, so use the other arm. This is a classic exam trap in dialysis questions.

front: A client on peritoneal dialysis has cloudy drainage fluid, fever and abdominal pain. What is suspected?
back: Peritonitis is suspected and it is reported urgently. Cloudy drainage is the early clue. Do not wait for the next exchange to see whether the fluid clears.

front: Why can an older adult become dehydrated with confusion as the first sign?
back: Thirst sense decreases with age, so older adults dehydrate easily and may not feel thirsty. Other signs include dry mouth, dark urine, fast weak pulse and dizziness on standing. Report new confusion instead of assuming it is baseline.

front: A client has crackles in both lungs, new shortness of breath and a weight gain of 2 kg in two days. What do you do?
back: Sit the client upright, check vital signs and oxygen saturation, report right away and slow the infusion only as policy permits. These signs suggest fluid overload. Continuing the same rate or speeding up could worsen breathing.

front: An IV site is red, swollen, cool and leaking. What does this suggest, and what do you do?
back: Swelling, coolness and leaking suggest infiltration, while redness and pain suggest phlebitis. Stop the infusion and report according to policy. Never keep infusing into a site showing these signs.

front: Why must you never speed up an IV to catch up without an order?
back: A faster rate can overload the client, especially older adults and those with heart or kidney disease. Check the order against client, solution, rate and time, and report a delay instead. Counting and recording the rate is part of safe practice.

front: Why is a new confusion always reported when sodium is abnormal?
back: Both low sodium (hyponatremia) and high sodium (hypernatremia) show up first as changes in thinking, and low sodium can lead to seizures. Normal sodium is about 135 to 145 mmol/L. Report new confusion even before results return.

front: Which losses commonly cause hypokalemia, and which signs does it produce?
back: Vomiting, diarrhea and some diuretics. Signs are muscle weakness, leg cramps, a weak irregular pulse, constipation and rhythm changes. Normal potassium is about 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L. Report these signs and abnormal results.

front: A client with kidney failure has muscle weakness and a slow irregular pulse. What does this suggest?
back: Possible hyperkalemia, which can stop the heart. Report immediately and do not treat it as simple fatigue. Failing kidneys cannot clear potassium, and some medications and tissue injury also raise it.

front: Why is potassium never given by direct IV push?
back: It can cause fatal heart rhythm problems. Potassium is always diluted and given by controlled infusion as ordered, and a high-alert medication check is part of safe practice. Direct IV push is never an acceptable answer.

front: A client reports tingling around the mouth and fingers and has muscle spasms. What electrolyte problem is suspected?
back: Low calcium (hypocalcemia), which can lead to seizures if severe. Report promptly. High calcium instead causes weakness, constipation, excessive urination and confusion, so the pattern of signs helps tell them apart.

front: A laboratory result is outside the normal range. What does the practical nurse do?
back: Check the client, compare with the last result and the condition, and report according to policy. Do not give or withhold a drug based on a lab value alone unless the order says so.

front: Why can sedation lead to respiratory acidosis?
back: Slow or shallow breathing lets carbon dioxide build up, which makes the blood acidic. Watch for drowsiness, confusion and slow breathing and report changes. Pain or anxiety with fast breathing instead causes respiratory alkalosis.

front: Which common situations are linked to metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis?
back: Metabolic acidosis occurs with diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney failure or severe diarrhea. Metabolic alkalosis occurs with prolonged vomiting. You connect situations to likely problems and report breathing, drowsiness and confusion changes.

front: Which signs point to diabetic ketoacidosis rather than simple high glucose?
back: Nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, deep fast Kussmaul breathing, a fruity breath smell, dehydration and drowsiness. It is an emergency needing IV fluids and insulin. Report right away and do not wait for the next glucose check.

front: An awake client who can swallow has a glucose below 4.0 mmol/L. What do you give?
back: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as glucose tablets or 150 mL of juice, then recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still low. Follow with a snack if the next meal is over an hour away. Report the event.

front: A client with low blood glucose is drowsy and cannot swallow. What is the safe action?
back: Give nothing by mouth. Call for help and follow the order or protocol for glucagon or IV dextrose. Giving juice to a drowsy client risks aspiration, which is a frequent exam trap.

front: Why is rapid-acting insulin tied to the meal tray, and why do two nurses check it?
